newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Challenges ahead for Lion - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Challenges ahead for Lion - analysts.

text.p: Analysts took little cheer from Lion Nathan Ltd's first half result on Monday and said the challenge lay ahead for the brewer in the form of its ongoing battle for market share with Australia's number one, Fosters Brewing.
While Australia would continue to be tough over the second half, analysts said they thought Lion may have laid proper foundations for an assault on Foster's dominant position.
Lion's first half earnings were NZ$72.2 million, down 20.8 percent on the same period a year earlier, but slightly above most share market forecasts.
Its annualised Australian market share was 41.1 percent by the end of February, against 42 percent six months earlier, but Lion said data from March indicated this had since improved.
Analysts expect Lion to report a full year profit of around NZ$120 million, down from $150.4 million in the August, 1996 year.
"The key to it is really Australia, and it's really whether they can match it with Fosters," analyst John Cairns at Cavill White Securities said.
Peter Sigley at SBC Warburg said it was too early for Lion's initiatives to show through in the first half.
"Once you start seeing the initiatives come through you may start seeing some of the benefits in terms of earnings as well as cash flows," Sigley said.
A depressed result, under a "do nothing" scenario, would have been very telling, he said.

"But they have made it clear that they are reacting to it. We know what their intentions are. Whether it works or not is the 64 million dollar question, but most of it seems to be logical, well-thought out sensible strategy," Sigley said.
Lion had reorganised its Australian operations with a more centralised focus to its five regional brewing operations there.
"The next phase will be to get a little bit of sustainable market share improvement through branding, and you won't see benefits of that for 12 or 18 months," Sigley said.
The Pepsico joint venture, which turned in a loss of just over NZ$5.0 million, remained a problem but Sigley said it was not intractable.
Analysts said the obvious solution was an amalgamation of the venture with Cadbury Schweppes in Australia. Such a deal would be difficult, Sigley added, but it was nevertheless logically sound.
"At the end of the day both parties have got to be sensible and some sort of deal will be nutted out to the benefit of both," he said.
One analyst, who declined to be indentified, said Lion had hung on to market share at a cost.
"What they are really banking on is getting strong growth coming up through the core brands," he said.
But at their NZ$3.42 close, down six cents on the day in thin turnover, analysts said Lion's shares remained fully valued given the unanswered questions peppering its outlook.
"Our recommendation would be to hold, but it's very much a matter of wait and see," said one.
-- Wellington Newsroom (64-4-4734746)
